chunks: From him, from Fadalah, from Saif ibn 'Amirah, from Abu Bakr al-Hadrami, from Abu al-Ward ibn Zayd, who said:

I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): 'Narrate a hadith to me and dictate it to me so that I may write it down.' He said: 'Where is your memory, O people of Kufa?' I said: 'So that no one may refute it back to me.' I asked: 'What do you say regarding the sacrifice of a Magian (Zoroastrian)?'
He said: 'In the name of Allah, then he slaughters.'
I said: 'A Muslim slaughters and does not mention (the name of Allah).'

He said: 'Do not eat it.' Indeed, Allah the Exalted says: 'So eat of that (meat) upon which the name of Allah has been mentioned, and do not eat of that upon which the name of Allah has not been mentioned.'

key_terms.بِسْمِ اللَّهِ: In the name of Allah, the invocation said before slaughter
key_terms.فَكُلُوا مِمَّا ذُكِرَ اسْمُ اللَّهِ عَل: So eat of that upon which the name of Allah has been mentioned (Quranic quote)
key_terms.مَجُوسِيِّ: Magian (Zoroastrian), referring to a follower of Zoroastrianism in Islamic jurisprudence

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating meat slaughtered by a Magian if they say Bismillah?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Istibsar*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes the validity of Zoroastrian sacrifices by noting their recitation of 'Bismillah,' distinguishing them from Muslims who omit the divine name, thereby rendering their meat impermissible. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that the explicit invocation of Allah's name is the critical condition for the permissibility of slaughtered animals, regardless of the slaughterer's broader religious identity. The narration underscores the practical application of Quranic dietary laws within the context of early Islamic interactions with Ahl al-Kitab.
